rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing retained compounds. This establishes a baseline for subsequent slope and temperature comparisons.

Test temperature selectivity while keeping the gradient unchanged, targeting the nearly coeluting late triplet and other unresolved pairs. Higher temperature should also provide time headroom for a shallower gradient if needed.

Change only gradient duration to measure slope sensitivity of the remaining critical pairs. This diagnostic run will show whether a shallower gradient separates the late close pair and the early triplet enough to justify its time cost.

Raise the starting organic fraction to remove low-organic time while using a shallower gradient to improve the slope-sensitive close pairs. Monitor the first peaks for compression as the gradient window narrows.

Explore the low-temperature, steeper-gradient region, where selectivity and elution order may separate the late triplet differently. The shorter gradient should keep the last peak below 10 minutes despite the lower temperature.

Test whether a higher starting fraction moves the early triplet past its selectivity crossover while permitting a shallower gradient for the late close pair. This should keep the last peak near 10 minutes, with early-peak compression the main risk.

Move beyond the early-pair crossover seen at phi0 0.20 while reducing gradient slope to improve the late close pair. The last peak should remain near 10 minutes; check whether the first three peaks retain sufficient separation.

Hold the best gradient fixed and lower temperature to shift the nearly coeluting early pair away from its crossover. This isolates the temperature tradeoff between early-triplet separation and the late critical pair.

Test the intermediate slope between injections 2 and 3, retaining the low starting fraction that better separates the early triplet. This should improve the critical pairs while placing the last peak close to the 10-minute penalty threshold.

Refine the best method with a slightly shallower slope, targeting better resolution of the remaining close pairs while keeping the last peak near 10 minutes. The final organic fraction remains above the estimated last-peak elution fraction.

Explore a substantially steeper gradient to see whether the late triplet separates on the opposite side of an elution-order crossover. This also tests a faster region not covered by the local refinements so far.

Test an earlier transition to the final hold, placing the late critical triplet near the gradient-to-hold boundary. This may change its selectivity relative to a continuous gradient; monitor the last peak for added retention time.

Test an intermediate temperature to rebalance separation within the early triplet while retaining useful late-pair resolution. The slightly steeper slope than injection 4 should offset the increased retention and keep the last peak close to 10 minutes.

Test the temperature midway between the recent 50 and 60 C runs to balance the two early-triplet gaps. Keeping injection 4’s gradient isolates the temperature effect on both that triplet and the late close pair.

Probe the lower-temperature selectivity branch at the most promising starting fraction, where the early close pair may separate beyond its crossover. The steeper gradient offsets the temperature-related retention increase and should keep the last peak near 10 minutes.

Test whether cooling relieves the early- and middle-pair compression seen at this starting fraction. Comparison with injection 7 will establish whether those gains outweigh the expected loss in late-triplet resolution and added retention time.

Refine the promising cooler, high-starting-organic region to improve the early triplet and middle close pair. A slightly steeper slope than injection 16 should bring the last peak back to approximately 10 minutes.

Slightly steepen injection 16’s gradient to bring the last peak below 10 minutes while preserving its favorable early-triplet selectivity. This targets removal of the time penalty with minimal resolution loss.

Use a slightly shallower gradient and a 5 C temperature increase to improve the late close pair while keeping the last peak near 10 minutes. This tests whether those gains outweigh modest compression of the early and middle critical pairs.

Test the remaining intermediate starting fraction with a slope expected to put the last peak near 10 minutes. This checks whether it balances early-triplet and late-pair resolution better than the two leading starting fractions.

Test whether a higher starting fraction and lower temperature move the remaining early and middle close pairs beyond their selectivity crossovers. This explores the neighboring region beyond the near-optimal phi0 0.25 methods, with early-peak compression as the main risk.

Lengthen the best broad-window gradient by one grid step to test whether improved critical-pair resolution outweighs the emerging time penalty. This brackets the optimum slope around injection 10 rather than changing selectivity again.

Slightly steepen injection 4’s gradient to remove its time penalty while preserving most of its resolution. This tests the best-timed version of the neighboring starting fraction against injection 10.

Test a slope of 0.04375 organic fraction per minute, just shallower than the best method’s 0.045. This finely brackets whether added late-pair resolution can outweigh a small time penalty near the 10-minute threshold.

Combine the favorable resolution balance at 55 C with a steeper slope of 0.05357 per minute, targeting a last peak just below 10 minutes. This final test removes injection 14’s time penalty while checking whether its early-triplet separation is preserved.
